title: Software timers and callback rules

spans.text: Goal: apply “Software timers and callback rules” to a real program or device. The key principle is: A software timer is not a precise hardware timer; measure jitter and scheduler load. In a project, follow this guidance: Set a short flag or send a message in the callback; move longer work to a regular task.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
The timer callback only notifies a task; the worker task prints the event to Serial Monitor.

A software timer callback runs in the timer-service task. Keep it short: blocking, lengthy Serial output, or expensive sensor work can delay every software timer. Send longer work to a worker task through a queue or notification.

Key line: `void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); if (xTaskCreate(timerWorkerTask, "timer-worker", 2048, nullptr, 1, &timerWorker) != pdPASS) { Serial.println("timer worker creation failed"); return; } sampleTimer = xTimerCreate("sample", pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000), pdTRUE, nullptr, timerCallback); if (sampleTimer == nullptr) { Serial.println("timer creation failed"); return; } if (xTimerStart(sampleTimer, 0) != pdPASS) { Serial.println("timer start failed"); xTimerDelete(sampleTimer, 0); sampleTimer = nullptr; } }`
What it does: A software timer is not a precise hardware timer; measure jitter and scheduler load.
Why it is used: Set a short flag or send a message in the callback; move longer work to a regular task.
If omitted or changed: The timer command queue can delay start/stop/reset requests when saturated.
